title: Pembina Pipeline Reports Voting Results from 2026 Annual Meeting of Shareholders
body_text: CALGARY, Alberta--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Pembina Pipeline Corporation ("Pembina" or the "Company") (TSX: PPL; NYSE: PBA) reported the voting results from its annual meeting of shareholders held virtually on May 8, 2026 (the "Meeting"). Each of the matters voted upon at the Meeting is discussed in detail in the Company's Management Information Circular dated March 19, 2026 (the "Information Circular"), which is available on SEDAR+ at www.sedarplus.ca , on EDGAR at www.sec.gov , and on the Company's website under Investors – Notice and Access at www.pembina.com . A total of 350,946,183 common shares representing 60.37 percent of the Company's issued and outstanding common shares were voted in person and by proxy in connection with the Meeting. title: PETMED EXPRESS D/B/A 1-800-PETMEDS ANNOUNCES ITS THIRD FISCAL QUARTER FINANCIAL RESULTS AND ITS QUARTERLY DIVIDEND OF $0.27 PER SHARE
summary: 1800PetMeds is your online pet store offering discount prices on pet supplies, medications, vitamins and supplements for your pet. Discount Prices on Pet Supplies, Nexgard, Bravecto, Trifexis, Simparica TRIO, Apoquel, and more.
body_text: PETMED EXPRESS D/B/A 1-800-PETMEDS ANNOUNCES ITS THIRD FISCAL QUARTER FINANCIAL RESULTS AND ITS QUARTERLY DIVIDEND OF $0.27 PER SHARE Gross Margins Improved Sequentially from 28.6% to 29.5% Net Income Margins Increased 180 Basis Points Sequentially Average Order Size increased from $84 to $85 Delray Beach, Florida, January 21, 2020 - PetMed Express, Inc. (NASDAQ: PETS) today announced its financial results for the quarter ended December 31, 2019. Net sales for the quarter ended December 31, 2019 were $59.9 million, compared to $60.1 million for the quarter ended December 31, 2018. Net income was $6.8 million, or $0.34 diluted per share, for the quarter ended December 31, 2019, compared to net income of $7.8 million, or $0.38 diluted per share, for the quarter ended December 31, 2018, a 10% decrease in diluted earnings per share. Average order size increased to $85 for the quarter ended December 31, 2019, compared to $84 for the same quarter in the prior year. Reorder sales increased 1.0%, to $53.8 million for the quarter ended December 31, 2019, compared to $53.3 million for the same quarter in the prior year. Menderes Akdag, CEO and President, commented: "We were encouraged with improvements to our average order size, and gross and net income margins during the quarter. Gross margins improved by 90 basis points from 28.6% in the September quarter to 29.5% in the December quarter. Net income margins improved 180 basis points from 9.6% in the September quarter to 11.4% in the December quarter. The gross margin increase can be attributed to our success in obtaining direct purchasing relationships with all the major manufacturers, and the implementation of the minimum advertised price (MAP) policy by those manufacturers. We anticipate MAP pricing to stabilize pet medication prices throughout the online channel. Net cash from operations for the nine months ended December 31, 2019 was $21.6 million. In 2020, we will focus on optimizing our marketing in this more competitive environment and being more efficient with our advertising spending. In addition, we will continue investing in our e-commerce platform to better service our customers. This platform will enable us to improve upon our already strong net promoter score of 84.0%. We believe this customer satisfaction measure reflects the strong bond we have with our customers and will assist the Company with future customer retention." The Board of Directors declared a quarterly dividend of $0.27 per share on the Company's common stock. The dividend will be payable on February 14, 2020, to shareholders of record at the close of business on February 3, 2020. The Company intends to continue to pay regular quarterly dividends; however, the declaration and payment of future dividends is discretionary and will be subject to a determination by the Board of Directors each quarter following its review of the Company's financial performance. This morning at 8:30 A.M. Eastern Time, Mr. Akdag will host a conference call to review the quarter's financial results. To access the call, which is open to the public, please dial (888) 455-1758 (toll free) or (203) 827-7025. Callers will be required to supply PETMEDS as the passcode. For those unable to participate in the live event, the call will be available for replay from 10:00 A.M. on January 21, 2020 until February 4, 2020 at 11:59 P.M Eastern Time. To access the replay, call (800) 964-3380 (toll free) or (402) 998-0979, and enter passcode 5500. Founded in 1996, PetMed Express is America's Largest Pet Pharmacy, delivering prescription and non-prescription pet medications and other health products for dogs, cats, and horses at competitive prices direct to the consumer through its 1-800-PetMeds toll free number and on the Internet through its website at www.1800petmeds.com . title: Anti-Money Laundering Compliance: Proven Strategies for 2026
summary: Anti-money laundering compliance in 2026 made practical. Learn proven strategies to detect risk, meet regulations, and protect business from financial crime.
body_text: Financial crime rarely announces itself, yet one weak anti-money laundering gap can quietly expose your entire business overnight. Criminal networks hid roughly $7.1 billion in suspicious transactions reported under U.S. AML requirements through late 2025, showing real systemic risk. As a bank, payment provider, or crypto platform, weak anti-money laundering compliance can suddenly expose you to costly financial crime losses. Manual monitoring, slow reporting, and fragmented controls make staying compliant feel like chasing threats you barely detect in time. Regulators increasingly expect stronger AML compliance management and accurate AML regulatory reporting, meaning you must modernize beyond basic internal rules. Understanding anti-money laundering fundamentals helps you reduce risk exposure, improve detection, and keep regulators confident in your controls. Mastering practical compliance strategies now positions your organization to stay ahead of enforcement pressure and operational disruption in 2026. Key Takeaways Anti-money laundering focuses on preventing illegal funds from entering financial systems through verified identities, monitored transactions, and accurate regulatory reporting. Banks, fintechs, payment providers, and crypto platforms must follow AML laws enforced through the BSA, PATRIOT Act, and federal oversight. Most AML failures come from outdated rules, manual reviews, reporting delays, and disconnected KYC and transaction systems. Scalable AML programs rely on risk-based monitoring, integrated reporting, reliable documentation, and continuous customer due diligence. What Is Anti-Money Laundering for Modern Business? Anti-money laundering for modern businesses refers to the policies, controls, and monitoring processes you use to detect, prevent, and report illicit financial activity. In practical terms, AML helps you verify customers, monitor transactions, meet AML laws, and file accurate regulatory reports while protecting your business from financial crime exposure. For banks, payment providers, and crypto platforms, AML is not just a legal requirement; it is a core risk management function that safeguards revenue, reputation, and operational continuity. Who Is Legally Required to Follow AML Regulations? Businesses that handle customer funds or facilitate transactions must prevent misuse under U.S. anti-money laundering laws. Here are the organizations legally required to maintain an AML compliance program in the United States. Banks and credit institutions must follow AML laws, monitor accounts, and file suspicious activity reports with regulators. Payment processors and fintech platforms are required to maintain AML compliance to detect fraud and unlawful transaction patterns. Cryptocurrency exchanges must apply AML and KYC controls to meet federal financial crime prevention standards. Money services businesses must implement AML programs to monitor transfers, remittances, and prepaid instruments. Companies processing high-risk or high-volume transactions face stricter AML regulatory scrutiny and reporting obligations. Regulated financial entities must document AML compliance programs to satisfy audits and ongoing supervisory reviews. Also read: 6th Anti Money Laundering Directive: Key Changes and Compliance Understanding who must comply only matters when you also know which laws and authorities enforce these obligations. AML Laws and Enforcement Businesses Must Prepare For U.S. regulators enforce anti-money laundering laws through multiple statutes that directly shape how your compliance program operates. Here are the key AML laws and enforcement frameworks your business must actively prepare for. The Bank Secrecy Act sets core AML obligations The Bank Secrecy Act requires you to maintain AML programs, monitor transactions, and file suspicious activity reports. Regulators assess whether your AML controls function effectively across customers, products, and transaction channels. The USA PATRIOT Act expands AML and KYC expectations The USA PATRIOT Act strengthened customer identification, due diligence, and information-sharing requirements for financial institutions. You must verify customer identities and understand ownership structures to prevent terrorist financing and money laundering. The Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2020 raises enforcement standards The AML Act of 2020 increased penalties and expanded FinCEN’s authority to evaluate program effectiveness. Regulators now expect risk-based AML compliance management aligned with real operational exposure. FinCEN enforces AML compliance through reporting accuracy FinCEN closely reviews suspicious activity reports for completeness, timeliness, and consistency across reporting periods. Weak AML regulatory reporting often triggers deeper examinations and enforcement actions. The Department of Justice targets systemic AML failures The DOJ increasingly pursues enforcement when weak controls enable repeated or large-scale financial crime. Senior management accountability increases when AML program deficiencies reflect governance or oversight failures. Regulators focus on how AML operates in practice Manual monitoring gaps, alert backlogs, and outdated rules frequently appear in enforcement findings. AML programs must evolve with transaction volume, payment complexity, and emerging financial crime typologies. Even with clear laws in place, many organizations struggle because compliance rarely works as expected in real environments. Where AML Compliance Programs Fail in Practice? Many AML programs fail because daily operational realities rarely match regulatory expectations or evolving financial crime behaviors. Here are the most common AML compliance breakdowns that expose businesses to enforcement, financial loss, and reputational damage. AML monitoring rules are outdated and fail to reflect current transaction patterns, products, and emerging financial crime typologies. Manual review processes create alert backlogs, causing delayed investigations and missed suspicious activity reporting deadlines. AML compliance programs operate in silos, disconnected from KYC, payments, and broader financial crime controls. Poor data quality leads to incomplete customer profiles, inaccurate risk scoring, and unreliable AML regulatory reporting. Teams rely on static AML policies that are not aligned with real business models or transaction behavior. Lack of automation increases operational costs while reducing the accuracy and consistency of AML controls. Compliance teams struggle to scale AML processes as transaction volumes grow across digital and cross-border channels. Weak governance and oversight prevent early detection of systemic AML failures before regulators identify them. Also Read: Comprehensive Guide to AML Compliance in FinTech Identifying failures is only useful when paired with practical ways to fix them without adding unnecessary operational strain. Practical AML Compliance Strategies That Scale Scalable AML compliance focuses on controlling risk efficiently as transaction volumes, customers, and regulatory expectations continuously increase. Here are the practical strategies businesses use to strengthen AML programs without slowing operations or increasing compliance overhead. 1. Align AML Programs With Real Transaction Risk Your AML strategy must reflect how funds actually move across customers, products, and payment channels every day. Generic risk models often miss transaction velocity, geographic exposure, and misuse patterns that regulators closely examine. Risk-aligned AML controls reduce blind spots and improve detection accuracy without creating unnecessary operational friction. 2. Build AML Controls That Scale With Business Growth AML programs often break when transaction growth outpaces monitoring capacity and investigation resources. You need controls that automatically adjust as customer volumes, payment flows, and risk exposure expand. Scalable AML compliance prevents alert backlogs while maintaining consistent oversight across high-growth financial environments. 3. Reduce False Positives Without Weakening Controls ‍ Excessive false positives overwhelm compliance teams and delay investigations into genuinely suspicious financial activity. Refined AML rules using behavioral indicators help separate legitimate transactions from higher-risk patterns. Lower false positives allow faster reporting and more effective use of limited compliance resources. 4. Integrate AML With KYC and Payment Systems AML programs perform better when directly connected to onboarding, identity verification, and transaction processing systems. Disconnected workflows create gaps between customer risk profiles and real-time financial behavior. Integrated systems enable faster risk assessment and more reliable suspicious activity reporting across customer lifecycles. 5. Strengthen AML Governance and Internal Accountability ‍ AML compliance weakens when ownership is unclear across compliance teams, leadership, and operational stakeholders. Clear governance ensures accountability for monitoring effectiveness, reporting accuracy , and regulatory communication. Strong oversight helps you detect systemic AML weaknesses before audits or enforcement actions surface them. Strong strategies still fall short if reporting gaps expose weaknesses that regulators quickly notice. AML Regulatory Reporting and Business Risk Exposure Regulatory reporting remains one of the most scrutinized elements of AML compliance, and poor reporting amplifies business risk exposure significantly. Here are the key risk realities shaped by AML reporting trends and enforcement data you need to know. Financial institutions submitted 20.5 million currency transaction reports (CTRs) , showing the sheer reporting scale your AML systems must manage. Late or inconsistent AML regulatory reporting continues to trigger regulatory scrutiny and deeper compliance examinations. Reporting backlogs often result from systems that do not scale with increasing transaction volumes across digital and cross-border channels. Inaccurate SARs contribute to enforcement actions and fines when regulators determine that reporting did not reflect underlying risk patterns. Regulatory reporting gaps slow your ability to detect high-risk behavior and protect your business from escalating financial crime exposure. Manual reporting processes increase compliance costs while reducing the speed and quality of submissions. Automated reporting tools integrated with monitoring systems help reduce delays and improve AML submission accuracy. Real-time data feeds enable better correlation between customer risk profiles and suspicious activity reporting needs. Effective AML reporting strengthens executive confidence and improves your ability to withstand regulatory reviews. Also Read: How AI-Powered Compliance is Revolutionizing Risk Management for Businesses How reporting is handled often depends on whether compliance relies on manual effort or automated systems. Manual vs Automated AML Compliance Compared The way you run AML compliance directly impacts detection accuracy, reporting speed, and your ability to scale without regulatory friction. Here’s a clear comparison showing how manual and automated AML approaches perform in real operating environments. Area Manual AML Compliance Automated AML Compliance Risk detection Rule-based, limited context Behavior-driven, contextual risk analysis Transaction volume handling Breaks under high volumes Scales across high-velocity transactions Monitoring coverage Periodic, delayed reviews Continuous, real-time monitoring Regulatory reporting Slow, error-prone submissions Timely, consistent AML reporting False positives High alert noise Reduced noise through smarter filtering Operational effort Labor-intensive reviews Streamlined investigations Audit readiness Fragmented documentation Centralized, audit-ready records Business scalability Requires more staff Grows without proportional cost increases AiPrise supports automated AML compliance by strengthening risk detection, simplifying reporting, and helping teams scale without increasing manual burden. Regardless of approach, accurate identity and document verification remain the foundation of effective AML controls. IDs and Documents Required for AML Compliance Effective AML compliance depends on verifying identities and business legitimacy using reliable, up-to-date documentation. Here are the key IDs and documents you must collect and maintain to meet AML requirements without slowing operations. Government-issued photo IDs, such as passports or driver’s licenses, confirm individual identity during AML and KYC checks. Proof of address documents, including utility bills or bank statements, help validate customer location and residency risk. Tax identification numbers, such as SSN or EIN, support identity verification and regulatory reporting accuracy. Business registration documents confirm legal existence and ownership structure for AML and KYB compliance. Beneficial ownership records identify individuals who ultimately control or profit from business entities. Financial statements provide context on business activity and help assess unusual transaction behavior. Transaction records support ongoing monitoring and enable accurate suspicious activity reporting. Sanctions and watchlist screening data ensure customers are not linked to prohibited individuals or entities. Updated documentation must be maintained continuously to reflect changes in ownership, control, or risk profiles. Also read: Anti Money Laundering and Procurement Risk in Insurance Sector Document checks alone are not enough without a deeper understanding of customer behavior and ownership risk. How Customer Due Diligence (CDD) Reinforces AML Effectiveness? Strong customer due diligence connects identity intelligence with transaction behavior to prevent financial crime before risks escalate. Here’s how CDD directly strengthens anti-money laundering outcomes for regulated financial businesses. CDD establishes verified customer identities, reducing anonymity that criminals exploit to move illicit funds through financial systems. Risk-based CDD helps you classify customers accurately, ensuring higher scrutiny for profiles with elevated money laundering exposure. Ongoing CDD monitoring keeps customer risk assessments current as behavior, geography, or transaction patterns change. Enhanced due diligence supports deeper investigation into complex ownership structures and high-risk business relationships. Consistent CDD improves the quality and accuracy of suspicious activity reporting by linking behavior to verified identity data. Integrated CDD workflows reduce gaps between onboarding, monitoring, and AML regulatory reporting processes. AiPrise strengthens CDD through its AI-powered identity verification, enabling real-time risk assessment and continuous monitoring at scale. Bringing all these elements together requires technology that supports scale without adding complexity. How AiPrise Supports AML Compliance at Scale Scalable AML compliance depends on combining accurate identity verification, risk intelligence, and ongoing monitoring within a single operational framework. Here’s how AiPrise helps you operationalize AML compliance without adding manual complexity. Business Verification (KYB) validates companies against global registries, confirming legal existence, ownership structures, and beneficial owners. User Verification (KYC) verifies individuals using government-backed identity checks, reducing anonymity risks during onboarding and account access. Fraud and Risk Scoring applies risk-based decisioning using behavioral, device, and identity signals to detect high-risk activity early. Ongoing Monitoring continuously tracks changes in customer behavior, ownership, or risk indicators to support dynamic AML compliance. Watchlist and Sanctions Screening screens individuals and businesses against global sanctions, PEPs, and adverse media lists. Case Management centralizes investigations, audit trails, and decisions, helping you respond faster during examinations and audits. AML-Ready Reporting Outputs support consistent suspicious activity reporting by linking identity data, transaction behavior, and risk decisions. When you treat AML compliance as a scalable, risk-driven system rather than a reactive obligation, you protect growth, trust, and long-term business resilience. Wrapping Up Anti-money laundering compliance in 2026 is no longer about reacting to regulations but about building systems that manage risk proactively and efficiently. When you align AML strategies with real transaction behavior, reporting expectations, and scalable controls, compliance becomes a business enabler instead of a constraint. AiPrise helps you achieve this by unifying AML, KYC, KYB, and risk intelligence into a single, scalable compliance framework. What is anti-money laundering (AML)? Anti-money laundering refers to laws, processes, and controls designed to prevent criminals from disguising illegal funds as legitimate income. 2. Who needs an AML compliance program? Banks, payment providers, cryptocurrency platforms, money services businesses, and regulated financial entities must maintain AML compliance programs. 3. What is an AML program? An AML program is a structured set of policies, procedures, monitoring systems, and reporting mechanisms used to detect and prevent financial crime. 4. What does AML mean in banking and finance? In banking and finance, AML refers to mandatory controls that monitor transactions, verify customers, and report suspicious activity to regulators.

title: Rethinking Calibration Standards: How EuroLoop Is Setting a New Benchmark with Ultrasonic Technology
summary: Discover how EuroLoop became the first gas calibration facility to replace turbine meters with ultrasonic technology, improving repeatability, diagnostics, and operational efficiency.
body_text: For decades, calibration facilities have relied on turbine meters as the reference standard for high-pressure gas measurement. Their repeatability made them the trusted backbone of custody transfer calibration where measurement accuracy directly impacts financial outcomes. But as the industry evolves, so do the demands placed on these facilities. Working closely with EuroLoop , one of the world’s leading gas calibration centers in Rotterdam, I’ve had the privilege of seeing firsthand what happens when a forward-thinking operator challenges the status quo and proves that a better path forward is possible. The Challenge: Balancing Accuracy with Operational Reality EuroLoop operates a world-class, closed-loop calibration facility where audit-ready, highly repeatable measurement is non-negotiable. Like many facilities, they traditionally depended on turbine meters as reference standards. While proven, these systems brought inherent limitations: Narrower operational range High maintenance due to moving parts and contamination risk Limited ability to automate and gain deeper process insight Lack of diagnostic tools At the same time, previous ultrasonic technologies simply couldn’t meet the repeatability requirements needed for reference measurement. This created a clear challenge: Could EuroLoop achieve turbine-level repeatability while unlocking the operational advantages of ultrasonic measurement? A Turning Point: When Performance Changed the Conversation EuroLoop’s evaluation process was rigorous and rightfully so. They had tested meters from manufacturers across the industry, benchmarking performance over time using watchdog meters within their calibration loop. What made the difference wasn’t just the inherent advantages of ultrasonic technology, it was repeatability . For the first time, an ultrasonic solution demonstrated the level of stability required to be seriously considered as a reference standard. That moment changed the conversation from “Is ultrasonic flow measurement viable?” to “How do we implement this with confidence?” From Validation to Transformation The transition didn’t happen overnight. EuroLoop took a phased, highly controlled approach—validating performance line by line before scaling across the facility. Ultimately, they implemented Emerson ’s Rosemount™ 3418 Eight-Path Gas Ultrasonic Flow Meters as their reference standard, supported by additional meters for continuous validation and traceability. This wasn’t just a technology upgrade; it was a fundamental shift in how calibration could be performed. Unlocking New Levels of Performance By moving to ultrasonic measurement, EuroLoop achieved several meaningful improvements: True Reference-Level Repeatability: Ultrasonic meters reached the repeatability required to replace turbine meters in reference applications—something that wasn’t previously possible. Broader Rangeability and Flexibility: With a wider linear operating range, EuroLoop was able to reduce line sizes from 16-inch turbine meters to 12-inch ultrasonic meters, lowering infrastructure requirements while maintaining performance. Lower Cost of Ownership: Eliminating moving parts significantly reduced maintenance and downtime challenges, an ongoing pain point with turbine-based systems. Increased Automation and Insight: Access to raw measurement data and advanced diagnostics enabled greater automation of calibration processes and deeper visibility into flow behavior. As someone who has worked closely with their team, one of the most impactful changes has been how much more they now see . From flow profile changes to system stability, ultrasonic diagnostics provide a level of insight that simply wasn’t possible before. A First for the Industry EuroLoop is now the first calibration facility to fully transition from turbine meters to ultrasonic meters as the reference standard. That’s a significant milestone not just for one facility, but for the broader energy industry. It demonstrates that calibration centers no longer must tradeoff between: Accuracy and flexibility Repeatability and automation Performance and cost efficiency Those trade-offs are no longer necessary. What This Means for the Future of Calibration From my perspective, this project represents more than a successful implementation, it signals a shift in what the industry should expect from calibration technology. With ultrasonic measurement, facilities can now: Design more flexible, scalable calibration systems Reduce operational risk tied to maintenance and downtime Leverage data to drive smarter, more automated workflows Maintain full traceability while improving performance And importantly, they can do all of this without compromising on measurement integrity . A Partnership Built on Trust and Performance One of the things I value most about working with EuroLoop is their commitment to rigor. They tested, challenged, and validated every step of this transition. That’s exactly what makes the outcome so meaningful. They didn’t adopt ultrasonic technology because it was new, they adopted it because it proved itself. Setting the Benchmark EuroLoop has set a new benchmark for high-integrity gas calibration—one built on confidence, data, and performance. As more facilities evaluate how to modernize their operations, I believe this project will serve as an example for what’s possible. And in many ways, this is just the beginning. title: Can GST Penalty Under Section 129 Apply Without Intent to Evade Tax?
summary: Can GST authorities impose a Section 129 penalty without proving tax-evasion intent? Understand the Balaji Traders judgment, legal position and taxpayer safeguards.
body_text: Can GST Penalty Under Section 129 Apply Without Intent to Evade Tax? Can GST Authorities Impose a Section 129 Penalty Without Tax-Evasion Intent? Section 129 of the GST Act is not meant to impose penalties in a mindless manner if there is some procedural flaw in the process of movement of goods. While considering a GST Penalty Under Section 129 , the authorities must examine the complete facts and documents related to the transaction. In the case of Balaji Traders v. State of U.P., the Allahabad High Court refused to uphold the imposition of a penalty on the ground that the authorities had not established that the taxpayer committed GST evasion and had less regard for the examination of documents relating to the transaction. The decision, however, does not mean that penalties cannot be otherwise imposed when it comes to missing or defective e-way bills. Rather, the eventual outcome of this issue would be determined by various factors, including the nature of the violation, existing documents, surrounding facts, and applicable legal precedents. What does Section 129 of the GST Act Cover? Under the provisions of Section 129 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017, detention of goods and vehicles while in transit is covered. This will be applicable when goods are being transported or stored in contravention of the law and rules made under this Act. The proper officer can detain both the goods as well as the vehicle, and issue the required notice stating the penalty and then pass a final decision in accordance with law. On a practical level, proceedings under Section 129 can arise when the following things happen: An e-way bill is either absent or not valid. The required invoice documents are missing. The goods being moved do not match the papers that are accompanying them. The vehicle, consignee or destination requires correction. There are concerns with regard to the proper declaration of the concerned transaction. It should be noted that a question of procedural breach may not necessarily be the same as a question of viability of the penalty involved. Read More: Case Laws on Sections 129 and 130 of the CGST Act, 2017 What is Mens Rea Under GST? Mens rea refers to the guilty mind or intention behind committing a violation of law. In a GST situation, intent to evade tax may include actions such as: Falsely hiding the movement of goods. Issuing fake or backdated invoices. Undervaluing the price or quantity of goods. Delivering goods to a secret entity. Reusing documents for different shipments. Keeping a transaction off the books. A mere clerical mistake, late preparation of documents, or lack of transport information cannot be equated with the intention. Is Intention to Evade Tax Expressly Mentioned in Section 129? The wording that can be found in Section 129 refers to the transportation of goods unlawfully and in contrary with the GST Act or the provisions of the Act. However, it does not state in each clause that intention to evade tax must be proved. Section 130 talks about confiscation separately, mentioning provisions related to serious violations involving intention to evade tax. This has led to a debate in the law as to whether each court violation can entail a penalty under Section 129 or whether the officer must examine the intent of the taxpayer and its implications on tax. In Balaji Traders, the Allahabad High Court reaffirmed its previous opinion about the need to prove intention to evade as an element in the case considered. Therefore, this decision should be understood in its factual and jurisdictional context, and not as an absolute national principle applicable to all disputes under Section 129. Section 129 vs Section 130 of the GST Act Basis Section 129 Section 130 Primary purpose Detention, seizure and release of goods in transit Confiscation of goods or conveyance General trigger Transportation in contravention of GST provisions Serious specified contraventions Main consequence Detention and statutory penalty Confiscation, fine and penalty Express role of intent Not stated in the same express manner throughout the provision Intention to evade tax is expressly relevant in specified situations Key taxpayer issue Whether the discrepancy justifies detention and penalty Whether the grounds for confiscation are established ‍ Read More: Case Laws on Sections 129 and 130 of the CGST Act, 2017 What Happened in Balaji Traders v. State of U.P.? On October 6, 2023, the Allahabad High Court ruled on the case of M/s Balaji Traders and Another v. State of U.P. and Others. The firm was registered as a dealer in cigarettes, pan masala and food-processing spices. The firm received an order from a dealer based in Nashik and raised a tax invoice dated November 18, 2022. The transportation of goods was to be carried out by railways. The firm claimed that the Railway Receipt number was necessary for the proper completion of the e-way bill. The owner went inside the Kanpur Railway Station to get the bookings done. The consignment, however, was kept in an e-rickshaw outside the railway station. Goods were seized by GST. As per the taxpayer, the e-rickshaw driver told the officials that the owner was inside the railway station with the requisite documents. When the goods were seized, a penalty of ₹5,58,286 was levied. What Was the Taxpayer’s Explanation? Balaji Traders maintained its position that the transaction was legitimate and was already supported by a tax invoice. The main points put forward by the taxpayer were: Tax invoice had been generated before interception. Goods were in transit through legal means by rail. Railway Receipt number is necessary to finalise the e-way bill. Owner was present at the place to finalise the rail booking. The driver of the e-rickshaw has notified the authorities regarding the matter. Subsequent to this, documents in support and explanation were provided. There was no intent to hide the transaction or avoid GST. The taxpayer further stated that there was no mention of any finding as regards the intention to evade tax either in any of the notices or in the order passed for levy of penalty. What Did the GST Department Argue? The Department argued that the required documents were not presented at the time of the seizure of the goods. It argued that the transport of goods without the necessary documents amounted to a violation of the Goods and Services Act. The Department also raised concerns over the transaction not being recorded in the case of the absence of interception of the goods. Thus, the High Court had to determine whether this suspicion was sufficient to impose penalties or whether the authorities were required to carefully assess the documents and explanations provided by the taxpayer. What did the Allahabad High Court Decide? The Allahabad High Court has rejected both the penalty order as well as the order passed by the Appellate Authority. The Court observed that the relevant authorities had failed to establish any finding against Balaji Traders. It also held that the explanation submitted by the taxpayer in relation to railway booking and the Railway Receipt number had also not been properly taken into consideration by the authorities. Judgment at a Glance Point Details Court Allahabad High Court Case Balaji Traders v. State of U.P. Decision date October 6, 2023 Main issue Section 129 penalty without a finding of tax-evasion intent Taxpayer’s evidence Existing invoice and railway-booking explanation Court’s concern Relevant facts were ignored and no intention to evade tax was recorded Result Penalty and appellate orders were quashed Additional relief Refund ordered, with interest for delayed repayment Why was the Penalty Quashed? 1. No Finding of Tax-Evasion Intent The notice and penalty order did not refer to the taxpayer's plans for evading the GST. A serious penalty cannot be levied based on mere assumptions that certain transactions have not been recorded anywhere. 2. Relevant Evidence was not Properly Examined It was clarified that the owner of the business was at the railway station arranging the documents related to the booking. It was expected that the authorities would check and provide reasons if they find this explanation unsatisfactory or untrue. 3. A Genuine Invoice Already Existed There was some documentation regarding the transaction. An invoice was created before the interception of the consignment. While an invoice is not sufficient, it can still serve as evidence that the supply was not totally hidden. 4. Procedural Lapse is Treated as Tax Evasion The evidence included: A phoney recipient. Concealed goods. Underreported value. Erroneous quantity. Repeated documents. An unregistered destination. Because the evidence was missing, the Court ultimately decided that the penalty order was invalid. What Relief did the Court Grant? The Supreme Court: Cancelled the penalty order issued on November 25, 2022. Cancelled appellate order was issued on March 24, 2023. Instructed the concerned agencies to return the fine and penalty money within 15 days. Ordered the payment of interest at the rate of 9% on any delayed payment. Levied costs of ₹1,000. Allowed to take recovery of costs from the official responsible. Does Balaji Traders Make Mens Rea Mandatory in Every Section 129 Case? Not necessarily. This ruling goes to show that legal support is available whenever the transaction is genuine, documents existed before interception, and the order imposing a fine does not contain any evidence-based finding on tax evasion. The fact remains that Section 129 provides a solution for cases when the goods are being transported against GST requirements. The legal implications in such cases might differ based on: The applicable High Court jurisdiction. The date of the transaction. Statutory amendments. The seriousness of the discrepancy. Whether the invoice existed before interception took place. Whether tax was charged. Whether documents were created retrospectively. The final judgments passed on the issue thereafter. The Balaji Traders case thus has to be interpreted as a fact-specific judicial protection against mechanical imposition of penalties and not as a green signal to the transporter to carry out transactions even without prescribed documents. When can the Balaji Traders Judgment help a Taxpayer? A taxpayer can get help from a ruling if any of the following is true: An actual invoice existed before the shipment took place. The supplier and receiver could be identified. The goods matched what was written on the invoice. Tax was charged or accounted for. It was a procedural error or could be explained. There were no signs of hiding anything. The taxpayer has a clear and immediately presented excuse. The authority has disregarded relevant proof. The penalty order does not reveal any intent to avoid tax. When May the Judgment Not Help? Balaji Traders may offer limited assistance where: No invoice existed before interception. Documents were generated only after the goods were detained. Goods differed materially from the invoice. Quantity or value was understated. The destination was different from the documents. The supplier or recipient was fictitious. The same e-way bill had been reused. Similar violations had occurred repeatedly. The taxpayer could not explain the discrepancy. Read More: Difference Between Tax Planning and Tax Evasion What Evidence can Prove the Absence of Tax-Evasion Intent? Businesses should preserve: Tax invoices generated before dispatch. Purchase orders and delivery instructions. E-way bill generation records. Portal screenshots and error messages. Railway receipts or transporter documents. Vehicle and driver details. GST return entries. Proof that tax was charged and accounted for. Communication with the recipient or transporter. Evidence showing that the goods matched the invoice. Contemporaneous records are generally more persuasive than explanations created after detention. What should Businesses do during Section 129 Proceedings? Respond to Every Allegation The notice reply should directly explain: Why the document was missing or incomplete. When the invoice was generated. When transportation commenced. Whether tax had already been charged. Whether the goods matched the invoice. Whether any portal problem occurred. Why the transaction created no risk of revenue loss. Request a Reasoned Order The authority should consider the reply and supporting documents and provide reasons for accepting or rejecting them. Preserve All Interception Records Retain copies of: Forms GST MOV-01 to MOV-07, as applicable. Driver statements. Inspection reports. Detention orders. Notices. Payment records. Appeal documents. Strengthen Dispatch Controls Before goods leave the premises, businesses should verify: Invoice number and date. E-way bill validity. Vehicle number. Recipient GSTIN. Delivery location. Product description. Quantity and taxable value. What the Balaji Traders Judgment Does Not Mean The decision does not mean that: An invoice automatically replaces an e-way bill. Goods can be moved before generating mandatory documents. Every procedural mistake must be ignored. Later document generation always cures non-compliance. Intent must be decided identically by every High Court. Businesses are protected where records are faked or backdated. The judgment primarily reinforces the need for fair, evidence-based and reasoned penalty proceedings. Conclusion The Allahabad High Court’s ruling in Balaji Traders v. State of U.P. shows that a Section 129 penalty should not be imposed mechanically without examining the taxpayer’s explanation, available documents and surrounding circumstances. Where a genuine invoice exists, and there is no evidence of concealment or deliberate tax evasion, the absence of a recorded finding on intent can be an important ground for challenging the penalty. Nevertheless, prevention remains safer than litigation. Businesses should ensure that valid invoices, e-way bills and transport documents are generated and available before the movement of goods begins. Frequently Asked Questions 1. Can a GST penalty be imposed when a valid invoice exists? Yes, because a valid invoice does not automatically replace other mandatory documents such as an e-way bill. However, the invoice may help prove that the transaction was genuine and already documented. 2. Is mens rea expressly required under Section 129? Section 129 does not expressly use the words “intent to evade tax” in the same manner as certain confiscation provisions. Courts have nevertheless considered intent relevant in several fact-specific penalty disputes. 3. What did the Balaji Traders judgment decide? The Allahabad High Court quashed the penalty because the authorities had not recorded any intention to evade tax and had failed to properly consider the taxpayer’s railway-booking explanation and documents. 4. Can a taxpayer generate an e-way bill after interception? Subsequent generation does not automatically cure the original violation. The evidentiary value depends on the timing, transaction records, and the reason for the delay. 5. Can Balaji Traders be cited outside Uttar Pradesh? It may be cited as persuasive authority, but its binding effect depends on the court or authority hearing the dispute. 6. What is the best defence against a Section 129 penalty? The strongest defence usually includes contemporaneous invoices, transport documents, tax records, portal-error evidence and a consistent explanation showing that the transaction was genuine. ‍

title: How to reduce staff turnover with artificial intelligence: what’s changing in HR
summary: Artificial intelligence is changing how HR teams retain talent. Discover what signals AI detects and how to act in advance, not in reaction.
body_text: The HR function has never had access to so much information as it does today. And yet, one of the most persistent challenges remains the same: detecting early on when an employee is dissatisfied or disengaged from their work. For a long time, the tools available to understand the real situation of people were limited: an annual climate survey, a performance review, the occasional one-to-one. The information existed, but it arrived too late. Artificial intelligence is transforming that reality. Today, HR teams can identify early warning signals, get ahead of situations that used to only come to light when they were already hard to reverse, and make decisions backed by data, not just intuition. The real cost of losing talent and why it keeps happening The cost of losing talent rarely shows up in a single budget line. It’s the knowledge that walks out the door, the processes that break down, and the time it takes a team to get back up to speed. According to data from Humand clients, organisations that keep their teams informed and connected recover up to three hours of productive work per person, per week a signal of how much sustained engagement is worth, and how much is lost when it’s neglected. Why does it keep happening? In part, because warning signals arrive too late. According to Deloitte’s Global Gen Z and Millennial Survey 2026 , which gathered responses from more than 22,500 people across 44 countries, nearly half of these workers say they feel burnt out at work. Burnout, when left undetected, leads to disengagement. And disengagement leads to turnover. The problem isn’t a lack of information. It’s that the information available doesn’t always reach the right people at the right moment to act on it. From intuition to insight: what AI brings to the table Until recently, understanding how an employee was feeling depended largely on a manager’s intuition, or on tools that only provided an annual snapshot of the situation. Artificial intelligence changes that logic. AI-powered systems can analyse behavioural patterns in real time: whether someone has stopped engaging with internal communication channels, whether their interactions with company platforms have dropped off, whether there are shifts in how they respond to pulse surveys. No single signal tells the whole story but together, they make it possible to identify situations that would otherwise go unnoticed. The result is a shift in model: from reactive management to preventive management. It’s not about predicting the future, it’s about acting on signals that already exist, but that until now couldn’t be read with sufficient speed or precision What’s concretely changing in HR teams Adopting artificial intelligence in HR isn’t just a change of tools. It’s a change in the type of decisions the function can make and when it can make them. More relevant communication for each person. Rather than generic messages to the whole organisation, AI makes it possible to segment and personalise internal communications based on each employee’s profile, team or situation. The result is greater participation and a stronger connection to what the company is communicating. Real-time engagement monitoring. Metrics such as the frequency with which people use internal platforms, participation in surveys and interaction with content make it possible to get a continuous read on the state of the team, not just a periodic record. A more strategic role for HR. When HR teams have ongoing information about the real situation of their people, they can act as a strategic business partner, not just an administrative function. The difference lies in having data that allows them to anticipate, not just record what’s already happened. How Humand is bringing AI to frontline teams Nicolás Benenzon, CEO and Co-founder of Humand, recently appeared on NYSE Floor Talk to discuss something concrete: how artificial intelligence is changing the work of HR teams in companies with deskless employees. In the interview, Nicolás introduced Sammy, Humand’s AI agent that resolves HR requests in real time: time-off requests, shift changes, payroll verifications, HR letters. What used to take days, Sammy resolves in seconds. In organisations processing more than one million tickets a year, that’s not a minor detail, it’s the time that HR teams get back to focus on their people. That is exactly the transformation this article describes. When the operational side is taken care of, the HR team can focus its attention on what truly moves the needle: detecting disengagement signals before they turn into resignations, acting ahead of time and supporting people at the moments that matter. AI doesn’t do the human work. It gives back the time to do it well. Watch the full interview

title: UNESCO partners with Coursera and launches free AI ethics course, developed in collaboration with LG AI Research, for learners and institutions worldwide
summary: Today, I’m proud to welcome UNESCO, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization, to Coursera as they launch their first free course, the Global MOOC on the Ethics of AI, which they built with LG AI Research.
body_text: Today, I’m proud to welcome UNESCO, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization, to Coursera as they launch their first free course, the Global MOOC on the Ethics of AI , which they built with LG AI Research. UNESCO has defined standards for responsible AI usage with the first global framework on AI ethics , endorsed by 193 countries. As AI adoption accelerates, this course helps learners and institutions put those principles into action and strengthen ethical decision-making on a global scale. “Principles alone do not build ethical AI, people do. Through this course, UNESCO is taking the next step in its leadership on AI ethics, translating the Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence into practical learning that empowers people to apply ethical principles throughout the AI lifecycle. This is how we move from shared commitments to meaningful action,” said Prof. Khaled El-Enany, Director General, UNESCO. Dr. Lim Woo-hyung, Co-Head of LG AI Research, said: “Through UNESCO’s Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, the international community has forged a shared consensus on what ethical AI should be; what’s missing is the practice. The real work is to carry ethics through the entire lifecycle—from product development to service operation. We hope this MOOC gives working developers and researchers the practical foundation to build a trustworthy AI ecosystem and turn responsible innovation into an industry-wide habit rather than an aspiration.” Global MOOC on the Ethics of AI Intermediate level · 9 hours The new course, co-developed by UNESCO and LG AI Research, teaches learners to recognize ethical risks, weigh competing priorities, and make more informed decisions about how AI is designed, used, and governed. The program focuses on real-world applications, guided by insights from global experts at Carnegie Mellon University, the University of Toronto, the Alan Turing Institute, and more. Hands-on projects show how to translate core concepts, including privacy, transparency, sustainability, and human autonomy, into practical decisions and policies. Available in 11 languages, this 9-hour course requires no advanced technical knowledge and is designed for learners across sectors, including university students, researchers, policymakers, and technology leaders. Upon completion, learners will be ready to make key decisions that ensure AI is studied, built, and adopted in more responsible and equitable ways. We’re honored to expand our partnership with UNESCO. For years, we’ve worked together to make high-quality learning more accessible for all through UNESCO’s Global Education Coalition and Global Skills Academy . Today, we’re bringing that mission to one of the world’s most pressing needs: empowering learners and institutions to adopt AI responsibly. Enroll in UNESCO and LG AI Research’s free AI ethics course today! Get started now

title: How to write a glamping business plan that attracts investors and guests
summary: Most glamping business plans focus on survival. Learn how to write one for growth that anticipates bottlenecks and attracts investors from day one.
body_text: How to write a glamping business plan that attracts investors and guests by Josh Genuth , Senior Content Writer | July 13, 2026 Reading time: 7 minutes Share Josh Genuth , Senior Content Writer Share A glamping business plan is the blueprint for scaling from one dome to a 20-unit retreat that runs without you. Most plans focus on survival; this one focuses on growth. It anticipates the operational bottlenecks, marketing challenges, and financial questions that come with expansion, building the solutions in from day one. A plan built for growth forces you to think past the initial setup. It defines how you will automate operations, diversify revenue streams, and build a brand that is not dependent on third-party booking sites. This document demonstrates to investors that you’re building a scalable business with long-term potential. TL;DR Define your unique value proposition first: location, theme, or accommodation type. Build your operational plan for 20 units, even if you’re starting with two. Integrate technology for guest check-in, communication, and cleaning from the start. Balance OTA distribution with a strong direct booking strategy to protect margins. Use dynamic pricing in your financial model, not flat seasonal rates. Your plan is a living document. Revisit it quarterly to track progress against goals. What is a glamping business plan and why you need one A glamping business plan is your strategic roadmap. It outlines your vision, defines your market, details your operational strategy, and projects your financial performance. For lenders and investors, it’s the primary tool for evaluating risk and potential return. For you, it’s the guide that keeps your decisions aligned with your long-term goals. Without a plan, growth is reactive. You add units when you can, hire staff when you’re overwhelmed, and solve problems as they arise. With a plan, growth is intentional. You know when to expand, who to hire, and what systems you need to support a larger portfolio. It’s the difference between running a hobby and building an enterprise. The 7 core components of a successful glamping business plan Structure your plan around these seven sections. Be direct, use data, and always connect your decisions back to your core business goals of profitability and guest experience. 1. Executive summary Write this section last. It’s a concise, high-level overview of your entire plan, designed to be read in five minutes. Include your mission, the unique experience you offer, your target location, key financial projections like startup costs and projected revenue for year one, and your primary goal. State clearly what you are asking for, whether it’s a specific loan amount or an equity investment. 2. Company description and unique value proposition Detail your legal structure (LLC, S-Corp, etc.) and ownership. Then, define what makes your glamping business defensible. Your unique value proposition (UVP) is the core reason a guest chooses you over a competitor or a traditional hotel. Your UVP can be rooted in: Location: Seclusion, unique views, or proximity to a national park. Accommodation: A-frames, geodesic domes, restored Airstreams, or treehouses. Theme: A focus on wellness, digital detox, romantic getaways, or family adventure. Exclusivity: High-end amenities, private chefs, or curated local experiences. Get this wrong, and you’re stuck competing on price alone. Get it right, and you build a brand that commands premium rates. 3. Market and location analysis Here, you prove there is real demand for your concept. Start with your target audience. Go beyond broad demographics like “millennials” and define their psychographics. Are they adventure-seekers, burnt-out city dwellers, or families looking for a unique vacation? Where do they live? What do they value? Next, analyze the local competition. Include nearby hotels, vacation rentals, and campsites. What are their rates, occupancy levels, and guest reviews? Identify the gaps in the market that your business will fill. Finally, justify your location. Explain zoning regulations, accessibility, and proximity to attractions. Discuss seasonality and your strategy for driving occupancy during shoulder seasons. 4. Operations plan Your operations plan should be built for the business you want in five years, anticipating future scale from day one. Accommodations and amenities: List the types of units and the specific amenities for each, such as a king-sized bed, private hot tub, or kitchenette. Detail common areas like fire pits, outdoor kitchens, or bathhouses. Specify essentials like Wi-Fi, power, and water solutions. Guest journey automation: Map every touchpoint from booking to post-stay review. Automate routine communication for booking confirmations, pre-arrival instructions with keyless entry codes, and check-out reminders. Schedule cleaning and maintenance tasks automatically based on reservation status. Using vacation rental management software with Automation Tools creates a consistent experience for guests and reduces manual work. Team structure: Outline the key roles needed to operate, even if you’ll be filling them all initially. Define responsibilities for guest services, housekeeping, maintenance, and marketing. This demonstrates foresight and a clear plan for delegating as you grow. Boost your short term rentals today Get started A guest arrives to a cold yurt because the propane tank wasn’t checked. A cleaner misses a turnover because of a miscommunication. These small operational failures, when managed manually, compound as you scale and erode your reputation. 5. Marketing and sales strategy Your glamping site is worthless if no one can find it. Outline a multi-channel strategy to attract and retain guests. Distribution channels: Start with a balanced approach. Use OTAs like Airbnb, Vrbo, and Booking.com for their massive reach, but make a direct booking strategy your long-term priority. A branded website cuts out commission fees and gives you ownership of the guest relationship. Build your own direct booking website to capture high-margin reservations and guest data for future marketing. Branding and online presence: Your brand is your reputation, reflected in everything from your photos to your guest communication. Invest in professional photography and videography, as it’s the single most important marketing asset you have. Maintain an active, visually-driven presence on relevant social media platforms like Instagram and Pinterest. Guest retention: The easiest guest to acquire is one you’ve already hosted. Build an email list from your direct bookings. Send targeted offers, share updates about the property, and create a loyalty program to encourage repeat visits. 6. Financial projections and pricing strategy Be conservative with your revenue projections and thorough with your costs. Investors look for realism, not just optimism. Startup costs: Itemize every expense required to open your doors. This includes land, permits, site preparation, structures, utilities, furnishings, and initial marketing. (See the table below for a checklist.) Operating expenses: Project your monthly and annual costs. Include staff salaries, utilities, insurance, property taxes, marketing spend, and software subscriptions. Revenue forecast: Project your revenue for the first three to five years. Don’t use a single Average Daily Rate (ADR). Build a model that accounts for seasonality, weekday vs. weekend demand, and local events. Instead of static rates, plan to use dynamic pricing. This approach adjusts your rates based on real-time market data to increase both occupancy and revenue. A revenue management tool can automate this process, adjusting prices across all your channels to fill occupancy gaps. 7. Appendix This is the home for all your supporting documentation. It adds credibility to the claims made in your plan. Include detailed financial spreadsheets, copies of permits, market research data, quotes from suppliers, and professional resumes for all owners. Glamping startup cost checklist Use this table as a starting point for your budget. Ranges will vary significantly based on location, scale, and quality. Cost Item Estimated Budget Range Land Acquisition / Lease $20,000 – $500,000+ Permits & Licensing $2,000 – $25,000 Site Preparation (Grading, Roads) $10,000 – $100,000+ Utilities (Water, Septic, Power) $15,000 – $150,000+ Structures (Per Unit) $5,000 (Bell Tent) – $100,000+ (Cabin) Furnishings & Decor (Per Unit) $3,000 – $15,000 Common Area Development $5,000 – $50,000+ Insurance (First Year Premium) $2,500 – $10,000 Technology & Software $1,000 – $5,000 Initial Marketing & Branding $2,000 – $10,000 Scaling your glamping business with the right foundation Your business plan should explicitly address growth. How will you go from 5 units to 15? What operational changes are needed? How will your marketing evolve? The biggest barrier to scaling is often the operational drag created by manual processes. The systems that work for three yurts will break at ten. Choosing scalable technology from the start is non-negotiable. A robust short-term rental management platform acts as your central nervous system, connecting your booking channels, guest communication, and operational tasks. As you add properties, the system absorbs the complexity, not your team. Use reporting and analytics to track key performance indicators like ADR, occupancy, and revenue per available night. This data is critical for making informed decisions about when and where to expand. Platforms like Guesty® are designed for this journey. They offer solutions like Guesty Lite™ for hosts starting with 1-3 properties, Guesty Pro™ for professional operators managing growing portfolios, and Guesty Enterprise™ for large-scale hospitality brands. The right foundation allows you to add units without proportionally adding overhead.
